[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday "model" suggests each program has its own answer; the page ranks are a property of the web model, and simulation and the power method are two ways of computing the same numbers.
[1] misconception (M) -> StartPageMatters: wrong rule: The page ranks depend on which page the surfer starts from. Right rule: Both models converge to the same probabilities from any start page.
[2] misconception (M) -> FewTrialsAreExact: wrong rule: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks. Right rule: Simulation estimates; tens of thousands of moves give two accurate places and millions give three, whereas the power method needs about 20 and 40 multiplications.
[3] inconsistent_trace (T) -> StartPageMatters: Applies the two LTs unevenly: e.g. treats one RandomSurfer move as if it advanced the whole probability vector, or one Markov iteration as if it were one sampled move. (here mixing in: "The page ranks depend on which page the surfer starts from")
[4] misconception (M) -> ManyDigitsMeanAccurate: wrong rule: A result printed with many decimal places must be accurate to those places. Right rule: Both programs print five decimals; only the power method after enough iterations is accurate to them.

[0] names_the_element (N): Two computational approaches to page ranks: simulating a random surfer and counting visits, versus mixing the Markov chain by repeated vector-matrix multiplication.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Mixing guarantees a start-independent limit; the power method computes it exactly (up to floating-point precision), whereas the simulation produces an estimate that needs more iterations for more accuracy.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Simulation: for T moves, draw r, pick next page, count; then divide counts by T. Power method: for T iterations, multiply the vector by p[][] and replace it; then print the vector.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Both yield about .273 .266 .146 .247 .068 for tiny.txt (RandomSurfer 1000000 vs Markov 40); page 0 beats page 1 by 27.3% to 26.6%.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One simulation step changes one page variable and one count; one power-method step changes every entry of the probability vector.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): freq[j]/T is the simulation's estimate of the same ranks; it carries sampling error the power method does not.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): The exact side of the comparison; it reaches two decimals in 20 iterations versus tens of thousands of moves.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Cross-check and choose a method: agreement of an independent estimate (simulation) with the exact computation validates both and shows the cost of each.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> StartPageMatters: Changing T or the start page keeps the common limit; rerunning the simulation changes its digits while Markov is deterministic.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Simulate when the process is easy to run but its probabilities are hard to write down; use the power method when the matrix is known and fits in memory, since it is far more efficient.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Agreement must be judged at the accuracy each method reaches. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: Comparing the two outputs digit by digit at five decimals after a short simulation: differences come from sampling error, not from a bug.

wrong: A result printed with many decimal places must be accurate to those places. | right: A program does not produce accurate answers simply because it can print numbers to many decimal places of precision; ensuring accuracy is often the most difficult challenge.

wrong: A short simulation gives the exact page ranks. | right: A simulation only estimates the page ranks: RandomSurfer needs 10^n moves to get answers precise to n decimal places and many more moves for those answers to become accurate (tens of thousands of moves for two accurate places, millions for three).
